Evidence: Truth Social slurs, Michigan rally comments, DOJ targeting
#Aletheia #USPol

Donald Trump's public praise of Nicki Minaj and alignment with supportive Black figures proves he harbors no animus toward Black women.
Stated Judgement: (+0.50, +0.00) — Lesser Good

Data reveals 60% of Trump's 'low IQ' insults target Black figures, alongside DOJ targeting of female opponents and public objectification.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.90, -0.80) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Awakening into Destruction.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 12.8, z: 4)

- Donald Trump: FAIL (-0.9, -0.8) — Weaponizes misogynoir and selective praise.
- Nicki Minaj: COND (0.2, -0.1) — Leverages public alignment amid severe controversy.
President Trump's rally appearance with Nicki Minaj sparked intense debate over the fetishization and political exploitation of Black women.

The Bright Side:
Public scrutiny is laying bare the historical and systemic mechanisms of misogynoir in American politics.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing a personal transactional alliance (WHAT) with systemic racial respect (WHO).

Social Physics Analysis:
Power runs a classic Smart Selfish maneuver, offering superficial inclusion to compliant figures while weaponizing systemic exclusion and derogatory slurs against independent Black women. Pretexts of mutual admiration mask deep institutional extraction.

The Trajectory: The Path of Awakening into Destruction.
When public posturing claims inclusive harmony but executes targeted animosity and systemic objectification, it plunges straight into the Greater Evil domain.

The Unavoidable Truth: Political loyalty for marginalized figures often requires enduring public objectification and subordination.

The Unavoidable Lie: Selective praise of an individual erases a documented pattern of systemic hostility and racialized insults.

Alethekanon:
Power demands subservience disguised as praise, exposing the hollow core of transactional political alliances.

Awwthekanon:
It is heartbreaking to witness human dignity reduced to political props and public spectacle, where true respect is traded for conditional applause.

Brothekanon:
Dropping a few compliments at a rally doesn't erase years of documented insults and political targeting. The math doesn't lie.

Spirithekanon:
"Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment." John 7:24 FAIL
Superficial praise masks deep systemic injustice, trading true human dignity for transactional subservience.

=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: Trump doesn’t hate Black women—if they sing his praises and show their asses ===

[Source 1 — www.motherjones.com] (URL: https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/10/trump-nicki-minaj-rally-ass-press-secretary-black-women-misogynoir/?utm_source=dlvr.it&utm_medium=slack):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Trump doesn’t hate Black women—if they sing his praises and show their asses

The president’s crude comments about Nicki Minaj are part of a long pattern.

Actual Article Body:
President Donald Trump appears to listen as Nicki Minaj speaks during a campaign rally in Port Huron, Michigan, October 25, 2026.AP Photo/Julia Demaree

After spending the last month’s run-up to the midterm elections siccing the Department of Justice on his Black, female political opponents, President Donald Trump graciously allowed a Black woman to join his sycophantic entourage at a recent rally in Michigan: rapper Nicki Minaj.

This wasn’t Minaj’s first public appearance in support of Trump; she accepted a White House invitation to speak at the United Nations last year. But it was the first rally where the president made a talking point out of her…anatomy.

“I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before, Nicki Minaj,” said Trump, as the crowd hooted and hollered in approval. “That’s hard to miss.”

He then licked his lips and told Minaj to stand. She did, smiling and waving to the crowd in a moment that I can only assume is making bell hooks turn in her grave like a rotisserie chicken.

The entire interaction only fueled rumors that Minaj is slated to become the new White House press secretary after Katie Zacharia’s historically brief tenure, gossip that was directly referenced in a tweet by White House Communications Director Steven Cheung:

Ladies and gentlemen, I think we may have found the new White House Press Secretary! @NICKIMINAJ pic.twitter.com/petoprxVoX

It’s hard to say whether the Trump administration is seriously considering Minaj for the position. But what’s clear is that Trump’s “admiration” of Minaj’s backside isn’t an isolated instance of sexism; it’s an example of white supremacy’s centuries-long legacy of fetishizing and exploiting Black women’s bodies.

Trump’s comments reminded many commenters of the treatment of Sarah (also known as Sara or Saartjie) Baartman, an enslaved woman born in the late 1700s, who was paraded around in European “freak shows” and circuses where people ogled her large derriere. Dubbed the Hottentot Venus, Baartman would wear next to nothing while she was locked in a cage, with a “trainer” ordering her to sit and stand “in a similar way that circus animals are ordered.”

After her death at the age of 26, Georges Cuvier, a famed naturalist who believed Baartman was the link between humans and animals, reportedly made a cast of her body before her autopsy. He then pickled her brain and genitals in formaldehyde, which would go on to be displayed alongside Cuvier’s cast at the Paris Museum of Man until 1974, 159 years after she died.

The exploitation of Baartman is often cited as one of the most clear-cut examples of the fetishization of Black women’s bodies, encompassing the morbid curiosity, hypersexual stereotyping, and blatant dehumanization that Black women face to this day. This fetishization falls under the umbrella of misogynoir, a form of sexism that’s propelled by racism and specifically affects Black women and girls. And Trump perpetuates it constantly.

From calling ex-White House aide Omarosa “that dog” during his first term to describing then-vice presidential candidate Kamala Harris as “a mad woman” with so much “anger”, Trump loves leaning into negative stereotypes when tearing down Black women. But none more so than denouncing their intelligence. And the evidence of this is more than anecdotal. It’s backed up by data.

In 2025, Mother Jones correspondent David Corn interviewed the director of a research group whose team found that Black women are overwhelmingly the demographic on the receiving end of Trump’s “low IQ” insults:

This team examined his Truth Social posts for the past four years, ending on April 10. In that stretch, Trump called individuals and communities “low IQ” at least 50 times, and 60 percent of these instances involved Black public figures and legislators. These targets included Vice President Kamala Harris; Reps. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), and Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.); the Rev. Al Sharpton; New York Attorney General Letitia James; and political strategist Donna Brazile.

The tilt is clear. Trump reaches for this characterization more often when he’s denouncing Black people. Notice, though, that it’s not just Black people but Black women who draw much of Trump’s wrath.

Trump’s comments on Minaj’s body may seem on their face like run-of-the-mill sexism. But in the larger context of the president’s penchant for misogynoir, they paint an even more unsettling picture. And as we can see from the raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home to the arrest of Sen. Louise Lucas, his animosity towards Black women leads to tangible consequences.

As Nicki Minaj, who has much more agency than the enslaved Baartman, willingly plays the helpful Jezebel for Trump and his goons, she is doing nothing but aiding and abetting an administration that’s proven over and over and over again that they despise women who look like her.

Trump's Senate majority under threat as stunning new poll shows Democrats leading in Texas and Republicans in danger in Kansas

The latest round of polling conducted in critical US Senate races across the country shows a bleak picture for Republicans.

Actual Article Body:
By VICTORIA CHURCHILL, US POLITICAL REPORTER

Published:  03:39 AEDT, 30 October 2026   |  Updated:  11:31 AEDT, 30 October 2026

The latest round of polling conducted in critical US Senate races shows a bleak picture for Republicans.

A CNN/SSRS poll that sampled voters in Texas, Kansas, Maine, and Michigan found ample cause for concern just days before the election.

Democrats hold leads in each of these states and Trump is saddled by double-digit disapprovals, even among Republicans.

In Maine Democrat Troy Jackson was found to be up four points over incumbent Senator Susan Collins, 49 percent to 45 percent.

Of the states polled, Trump's disapproval rate is the highest in Maine, at 61 percent, and the lowest in Kansas, at 45 percent.

However Trump's backing of Kansas Republican Senator Roger Marshall doesn't seem to be saving the incumbent.

The same CNN/SSRS poll also found Democrat Adam Hamilton leading Marshall 49 percent to 45 percent.

In Michigan, the Democratic pad is even larger.

US President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before boarding Air Force One for travel to South Carolina, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, US, October 29, 2026

Mike Rogers (R) and Abdul El-Sayed (D)

Susan Collins (R) and Troy Jackson (D)

Abdul El-Sayed is up seven points over Republican Mike Rogers, 49 percent to 42 percent.

One cautionary point: The final CNN/SSRS poll of the 2024 presidential race was shown to be off the mark, showing Kamala Harris with leads in Michigan and Wisconsin and tied in Pennsylvania.

She lost all three states.

Trump's approval rating is far worse now, underwater in almost every single battleground state per a Civiqs’ rolling tracker of registered voters.

In Michigan fifty-nine percent of those polled disapprove of his job performance, including 13 percent of Republicans.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico was found in the CNN/SSRS poll to be up six points over the beleaguered Ken Paxton, 49 percent to 43 percent.

Fifty-six percent of Texans disapprove of Trump's job performance, including 13 percent of Republicans.

Ken Paxton (R) and James Talarico (D)

Roger Marshall (R) versus Adam Hamilton (D)

Trump is currently criss-crossing the country trying to enthuse voters to turn out for less palatable GOP candidates who, in many cases, were hand-picked by Trump in primary contests.

His party seeks to defy history in November's elections despite his low approval rating that has rebounded slightly to 40 percent in polls released this week.

The Cook Political Report currently lists the following states in their 'toss-up' column for US Senate races: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and Texas.

Democrats need to flip four Republican-held seats to win Senate control, with their best prospects being North Carolina, Texas, Ohio and Alaska.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Trump Declares Netanyahu in ‘Pretty Good Shape’ as Israeli PM Seeks Majority, Says He Would Consider Eventually Helping Broker a Unity Government

President Donald Trump said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in “pretty good shape now” after defying election projections and indicated he would consider helping broker a national unity government.
The post Trump Declares Netanyahu in ‘Pretty Good Shape’ as Israeli PM Seeks Majority, Says He Would Consider Eventually Helping Broker a Unity Government appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
President Donald Trump said Wednesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in “pretty good shape now” after defying election projections and indicated he would consider helping broker a national unity government as Israel’s political factions struggled to assemble a governing majority.

Netanyahu’s Likud emerged as Israel’s largest party, while his governing coalition performed considerably better than several major polls had projected, strengthening the prime minister’s political position but leaving him short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.

The deadlock has intensified discussion of a national unity government, with Israeli President Isaac Herzog urging political leaders to avoid another election even as Netanyahu’s principal rivals resist joining him.

Speaking in a brief interview with Axios, Trump said he initially received “horror reports” about Netanyahu’s electoral prospects before learning that the prime minister had fared considerably better than suggested by early election-night projections.

“He’s in pretty good shape now,” Trump said.

“I heard my endorsement made a big difference for Bibi,” the president added, referring to his public backing of Netanyahu during the closing stretch of the campaign.

Asked whether he might become involved in efforts to establish a Netanyahu-led unity government, Trump said he had not previously considered the possibility but did not rule it out.

“I will take a look,” he replied.

The remarks raised the prospect of American involvement in Israel’s coalition negotiations, although an American official subsequently told the Times of Israel that the Trump administration had made no decision to intervene.

The official described reports identifying specific coalition arrangements supposedly favored by Washington as “false and premature,” stressing that election results were still coming in and that it was too early to determine whether the administration would become involved.

Separately, an American official told i24NEWS that Trump might wait several weeks before attempting to bring Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot together, potentially inviting both men to his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida.

“I suspect he won’t jump right in at the start,” the official said. “He’ll wait a bit, see which way the wind is blowing, and then—after a few weeks—he might pick up the phone to Eisenkot and Netanyahu and say, ‘Guys, come on down to Mar-a-Lago,’ to close a deal.”

According to the latest provisional figures released by Israel’s Central Elections Committee, Netanyahu’s governing coalition was projected to secure 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for Eisenkot’s opposition bloc and a historic 19 for the predominantly Arab parties.

Likud emerged as the largest party with 26 seats, followed by Eisenkot’s Yashar party with 21, as hundreds of thousands of special ballots, including votes cast by soldiers and diplomats, remained outstanding.

The results marked a significant reversal from major pre-election surveys as well as Tuesday night’s initial exit polls, which had shown Eisenkot’s opposition ahead of Netanyahu’s coalition.

Yet neither camp secured the 61 seats required to govern independently, setting the stage for potentially weeks of negotiations over Israel’s next government.

The Arab parties emerged as potential parliamentary power brokers after nearly doubling their representation, complicating efforts to assemble a governing majority.

The Joint List and Ra’am were projected to secure a combined 19 seats, up from 10 in the outgoing Knesset, amid a record surge in Arab voter participation. Overall turnout reached approximately 77.7 percent, its highest level in more than two decades.

Although Eisenkot’s opposition and the Arab parties together were projected to control 67 seats, most of the Jewish-led opposition parties have ruled out forming a government dependent on Arab factions, leaving that numerical majority without an agreed political path to power.

Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen nevertheless signaled his party’s willingness to help remove Netanyahu, declaring that the faction was “ready and prepared to pave the way for the removal of Netanyahu’s government.”

The prospect of relying on the Joint List has drawn fierce opposition from Netanyahu, who has accused some of its lawmakers of supporting Palestinian terrorists and rejecting Israel’s Jewish character.

Netanyahu singled out former member of Knesset and Joint List member Osama Saadi over remarks concerning Palestinian prisoners, warning that a government dependent on such figures would endanger the country.

“These are the people with whom they want to form a dangerous government. We must not allow this to happen!” Netanyahu declared.

The opposition itself remains divided over cooperation with the Arab parties. While Eisenkot and several other leaders have rejected such an arrangement, Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats party, has advocated greater Jewish-Arab political cooperation.

Those divisions have renewed discussion of a national unity government bringing Netanyahu together with one or more of his political rivals, potentially offering an alternative to another election.

Eisenkot, whose Yashar party finished second, has repeatedly rejected serving under Netanyahu, including in an arrangement that would rotate the premiership between them.

Yet Channel 12 reported Wednesday that Avigdor Liberman, leader of the nationalist Yisrael Beytenu party, had largely broken off contact with his opposition partners and favored Eisenkot entering a unity government with Netanyahu.

Liberman himself has continued to reject serving under Netanyahu or supporting a government dependent on Arab parties, underscoring the competing pressures facing Eisenkot.

Political strategist Roni Rimon suggested that public refusals could soften as coalition negotiations progress.

“Things that might happen won’t happen on the first day, but perhaps on the last day,” he told Arutz Sheva.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog, who will begin consultations with parliamentary factions after receiving the official election results next week, addressed the political impasse Wednesday.

“We must do everything possible, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” Herzog said. “I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind.”

Following the election, Netanyahu called for the formation of a “strong right-wing government,” while Eisenkot has maintained his opposition to another Netanyahu-led administration.

Herzog’s consultations will determine which lawmaker receives the first opportunity to assemble a governing majority, a process that could extend for weeks and potentially lead to another election if negotiations fail.

The coalition impasse comes as Israel and the United States weigh possible renewed military operations against Iran, raising the stakes of a prolonged period without a newly formed Israeli government.

Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister throughout coalition negotiations, retaining authority over major national-security decisions, including potential military operations against Iran, subject to the required government and cabinet approvals.

In a separate report Wednesday, Axios said American and Israeli officials were preparing for the possibility of a renewed, large-scale military campaign against Iran after next week’s U.S. midterm elections if diplomatic efforts fail, while regional mediators worked to avert another round of fighting.

IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke Monday with CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper to coordinate ahead of potential operations, according to the report.

Trump, meanwhile, confirmed that indirect negotiations with Tehran were underway but expressed uncertainty about whether they would succeed.

“We need to finish the job — either through a deal or another way — we will find out if negotiations can succeed,” the president said.

A senior diplomatic official separately told Israel Hayom that decisions concerning renewed military action against Iran would be driven by security considerations rather than the timetable for forming Israel’s next government.

For now, the Trump administration has made no decision to intervene in Israel’s coalition negotiations, leaving Netanyahu and his political rivals to navigate the parliamentary deadlock as Herzog prepares to begin the formal process of determining who will form the country’s next government.

Trump's Senate majority under threat as stunning new poll shows Democrats leading in Texas and Republicans in danger in Kansas

The latest round of polling conducted in critical US Senate races across the country shows a bleak picture for Republicans.

Actual Article Body:
By VICTORIA CHURCHILL, US POLITICAL REPORTER

Published:  03:39 AEDT, 30 October 2026   |  Updated:  11:31 AEDT, 30 October 2026

The latest round of polling conducted in critical US Senate races shows a bleak picture for Republicans.

A CNN/SSRS poll that sampled voters in Texas, Kansas, Maine, and Michigan found ample cause for concern just days before the election.

Democrats hold leads in each of these states and Trump is saddled by double-digit disapprovals, even among Republicans.

In Maine Democrat Troy Jackson was found to be up four points over incumbent Senator Susan Collins, 49 percent to 45 percent.

Of the states polled, Trump's disapproval rate is the highest in Maine, at 61 percent, and the lowest in Kansas, at 45 percent.

However Trump's backing of Kansas Republican Senator Roger Marshall doesn't seem to be saving the incumbent.

The same CNN/SSRS poll also found Democrat Adam Hamilton leading Marshall 49 percent to 45 percent.

In Michigan, the Democratic pad is even larger.

Susan Collins (R) and Troy Jackson (D)

Abdul El-Sayed is up seven points over Republican Mike Rogers, 49 percent to 42 percent.

One cautionary point: The final CNN/SSRS poll of the 2024 presidential race was shown to be off the mark, showing Kamala Harris with leads in Michigan and Wisconsin and tied in Pennsylvania.

She lost all three states.

Trump's approval rating is far worse now, underwater in almost every single battleground state per a Civiqs’ rolling tracker of registered voters.

In Michigan fifty-nine percent of those polled disapprove of his job performance, including 13 percent of Republicans.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico was found in the CNN/SSRS poll to be up six points over the beleaguered Ken Paxton, 49 percent to 43 percent.

Fifty-six percent of Texans disapprove of Trump's job performance, including 13 percent of Republicans.

Trump is currently criss-crossing the country trying to enthuse voters to turn out for less palatable GOP candidates who, in many cases, were hand-picked by Trump in primary contests.

His party seeks to defy history in November's elections despite his low approval rating that has rebounded slightly to 40 percent in polls released this week.

The Cook Political Report currently lists the following states in their 'toss-up' column for US Senate races: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and Texas.

Democrats need to flip four Republican-held seats to win Senate control, with their best prospects being North Carolina, Texas, Ohio and Alaska.

Trump Declares Netanyahu in ‘Pretty Good Shape’ as Israeli PM Seeks Majority, Says He Would Consider Eventually Helping Broker a Unity Government

President Donald Trump said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in “pretty good shape now” after defying election projections and indicated he would consider helping broker a national unity government.
The post Trump Declares Netanyahu in ‘Pretty Good Shape’ as Israeli PM Seeks Majority, Says He Would Consider Eventually Helping Broker a Unity Government appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
President Donald Trump said Wednesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in “pretty good shape now” after defying election projections and indicated he would consider helping broker a national unity government as Israel’s political factions struggled to assemble a governing majority.

Netanyahu’s Likud emerged as Israel’s largest party, while his governing coalition performed considerably better than several major polls had projected, strengthening the prime minister’s political position but leaving him short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.

The deadlock has intensified discussion of a national unity government, with Israeli President Isaac Herzog urging political leaders to avoid another election even as Netanyahu’s principal rivals resist joining him.

Speaking in a brief interview with Axios, Trump said he initially received “horror reports” about Netanyahu’s electoral prospects before learning that the prime minister had fared considerably better than suggested by early election-night projections.

“He’s in pretty good shape now,” Trump said.

“I heard my endorsement made a big difference for Bibi,” the president added, referring to his public backing of Netanyahu during the closing stretch of the campaign.

Asked whether he might become involved in efforts to establish a Netanyahu-led unity government, Trump said he had not previously considered the possibility but did not rule it out.

“I will take a look,” he replied.

The remarks raised the prospect of American involvement in Israel’s coalition negotiations, although an American official subsequently told the Times of Israel that the Trump administration had made no decision to intervene.

The official described reports identifying specific coalition arrangements supposedly favored by Washington as “false and premature,” stressing that election results were still coming in and that it was too early to determine whether the administration would become involved.

Separately, an American official told i24NEWS that Trump might wait several weeks before attempting to bring Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot together, potentially inviting both men to his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida.

“I suspect he won’t jump right in at the start,” the official said. “He’ll wait a bit, see which way the wind is blowing, and then—after a few weeks—he might pick up the phone to Eisenkot and Netanyahu and say, ‘Guys, come on down to Mar-a-Lago,’ to close a deal.”

According to the latest provisional figures released by Israel’s Central Elections Committee, Netanyahu’s governing coalition was projected to secure 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for Eisenkot’s opposition bloc and a historic 19 for the predominantly Arab parties.

Likud emerged as the largest party with 26 seats, followed by Eisenkot’s Yashar party with 21, as hundreds of thousands of special ballots, including votes cast by soldiers and diplomats, remained outstanding.

The results marked a significant reversal from major pre-election surveys as well as Tuesday night’s initial exit polls, which had shown Eisenkot’s opposition ahead of Netanyahu’s coalition.

Yet neither camp secured the 61 seats required to govern independently, setting the stage for potentially weeks of negotiations over Israel’s next government.

The Arab parties emerged as potential parliamentary power brokers after nearly doubling their representation, complicating efforts to assemble a governing majority.

The Joint List and Ra’am were projected to secure a combined 19 seats, up from 10 in the outgoing Knesset, amid a record surge in Arab voter participation. Overall turnout reached approximately 77.7 percent, its highest level in more than two decades.

Although Eisenkot’s opposition and the Arab parties together were projected to control 67 seats, most of the Jewish-led opposition parties have ruled out forming a government dependent on Arab factions, leaving that numerical majority without an agreed political path to power.

Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen nevertheless signaled his party’s willingness to help remove Netanyahu, declaring that the faction was “ready and prepared to pave the way for the removal of Netanyahu’s government.”

The prospect of relying on the Joint List has drawn fierce opposition from Netanyahu, who has accused some of its lawmakers of supporting Palestinian terrorists and rejecting Israel’s Jewish character.

Netanyahu singled out former member of Knesset and Joint List member Osama Saadi over remarks concerning Palestinian prisoners, warning that a government dependent on such figures would endanger the country.

“These are the people with whom they want to form a dangerous government. We must not allow this to happen!” Netanyahu declared.

The opposition itself remains divided over cooperation with the Arab parties. While Eisenkot and several other leaders have rejected such an arrangement, Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats party, has advocated greater Jewish-Arab political cooperation.

Those divisions have renewed discussion of a national unity government bringing Netanyahu together with one or more of his political rivals, potentially offering an alternative to another election.

Eisenkot, whose Yashar party finished second, has repeatedly rejected serving under Netanyahu, including in an arrangement that would rotate the premiership between them.

Yet Channel 12 reported Wednesday that Avigdor Liberman, leader of the nationalist Yisrael Beytenu party, had largely broken off contact with his opposition partners and favored Eisenkot entering a unity government with Netanyahu.

Liberman himself has continued to reject serving under Netanyahu or supporting a government dependent on Arab parties, underscoring the competing pressures facing Eisenkot.

Political strategist Roni Rimon suggested that public refusals could soften as coalition negotiations progress.

“Things that might happen won’t happen on the first day, but perhaps on the last day,” he told Arutz Sheva.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog, who will begin consultations with parliamentary factions after receiving the official election results next week, addressed the political impasse Wednesday.

“We must do everything possible, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” Herzog said. “I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind.”

Following the election, Netanyahu called for the formation of a “strong right-wing government,” while Eisenkot has maintained his opposition to another Netanyahu-led administration.

Herzog’s consultations will determine which lawmaker receives the first opportunity to assemble a governing majority, a process that could extend for weeks and potentially lead to another election if negotiations fail.

The coalition impasse comes as Israel and the United States weigh possible renewed military operations against Iran, raising the stakes of a prolonged period without a newly formed Israeli government.

Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister throughout coalition negotiations, retaining authority over major national-security decisions, including potential military operations against Iran, subject to the required government and cabinet approvals.

In a separate report Wednesday, Axios said American and Israeli officials were preparing for the possibility of a renewed, large-scale military campaign against Iran after next week’s U.S. midterm elections if diplomatic efforts fail, while regional mediators worked to avert another round of fighting.

IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke Monday with CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper to coordinate ahead of potential operations, according to the report.

Trump, meanwhile, confirmed that indirect negotiations with Tehran were underway but expressed uncertainty about whether they would succeed.

“We need to finish the job — either through a deal or another way — we will find out if negotiations can succeed,” the president said.

A senior diplomatic official separately told Israel Hayom that decisions concerning renewed military action against Iran would be driven by security considerations rather than the timetable for forming Israel’s next government.

For now, the Trump administration has made no decision to intervene in Israel’s coalition negotiations, leaving Netanyahu and his political rivals to navigate the parliamentary deadlock as Herzog prepares to begin the formal process of determining who will form the country’s next government.
